Anne was certain to have more chances to observe them. Soon she had seen all four together often enough to form her own view. She was too wise to share it at home, knowing it would please neither the husband nor the wife there. She thought Louisa was the favourite, but, judging cautiously from her memories and experience, she did not believe Captain Wentworth was in love with either girl. Their feelings for him were stronger, though even these were not love. They were caught up in a brief excitement of admiration. Still, for one or more of them, it could—and probably would—turn into love. Charles Hayter seemed to realise that he was being pushed aside, yet Henrietta sometimes looked unsure which man she preferred. Anne wished she could make them all understand their own behaviour and the unhappiness it might cause. She did not think anyone was acting dishonestly. She found particular comfort in believing Captain Wentworth had no idea how much pain he was causing. Nothing in his manner suggested triumph, or any mean pleasure in defeating a rival. He had probably never heard of Charles Hayter’s hopes, let alone considered them. His fault lay only in accepting—and accepting was certainly the word—the attentions of two young women at the same time.

After a short struggle, Charles Hayter appeared to give up. He stayed away from Uppercross for three whole days, a striking change. He even turned down a proper invitation to dinner. On that occasion, Mr. Musgrove found him sitting with several large books in front of him. Mr. and Mrs. Musgrove were convinced something was wrong and spoke gravely of his working himself to death over his studies. Mary hoped and believed Henrietta had rejected him outright. Her husband, meanwhile, kept expecting him to arrive the next day. Anne could only feel that Charles Hayter was being sensible.

Around this time, one morning when Charles Musgrove and Captain Wentworth had gone out shooting together, the sisters at the Cottage were sitting quietly with their sewing. The sisters from the large house came to visit them at the window.

The November weather was beautiful. The Miss Musgroves walked through the small grounds and stopped simply to say that they were going on a long walk, so they supposed Mary would not want to join them. Annoyed that they seemed to doubt her ability to walk far, Mary immediately answered, ‘Oh yes, I would love to come. I am very fond of long walks.’ Their expressions convinced Anne that this was exactly what the girls had not wanted. She wondered again at the obligation created by this family’s habits: everyone must be told everything, and everything must be done together, however inconvenient or unwelcome.

‘I wish we owned a donkey. What we should do is all arrive on donkeys—Jane, Miss Bates, and myself—with my dear husband walking beside us. I really must speak to him about buying one. I consider a donkey practically essential to country life. However many ways a woman has to occupy herself, she cannot spend all her time shut indoors. And as for long walks, you know, there is dust in summer and mud in winter.’

‘You will encounter neither between Highbury and Donwell. Donwell Lane is never dusty, and at present it is quite dry. But come on a donkey if you like. Mrs. Cole can lend you hers. I should like everything to suit you as well as possible.’

‘I am certain you would. Believe me, my good friend, I give you full credit. Beneath that peculiar dry, blunt manner, I know you have the warmest of hearts. As I say to Mr. E., you are such an eccentric. Yes, Knightley, believe me, I fully appreciate how much thought you have given to pleasing me with this whole arrangement. You have chosen exactly what I would enjoy.’

Mr. Knightley had a further reason for avoiding a table in the shade. He wanted Mr. Woodhouse to attend as well as Emma, and knew that the sight of any of them sitting outdoors to eat would inevitably make him feel ill. Mr. Woodhouse must not be lured into misery by an attractive promise of a morning drive and an hour or two at Donwell.

The invitation was entirely sincere. No concealed terrors would make him regret having trusted it so readily. He agreed to come. He had not visited Donwell for two years. ‘On some particularly fine morning, he and Emma and Harriet could easily go. He could sit quietly with Mrs. Weston while the dear girls explored the gardens. Surely they could not be damp now, in the middle of the day. He would very much enjoy seeing the old house again, and would be delighted to meet Mr. and Mrs. Elton and any other neighbours. He could see no objection at all to going with Emma and Harriet on a really fine morning. It was very thoughtful of Mr. Knightley to invite them, very kind and sensible, and a much better idea than dining away from home. He was not fond of dining out.’

Everyone accepted so willingly that Mr. Knightley could count himself fortunate. The invitation met with such enthusiasm everywhere that they all seemed, like Mrs. Elton, to regard the scheme as a special compliment to themselves. Emma and Harriet said they expected to enjoy it immensely. Without being asked, Mr. Weston promised to bring Frank over if possible, a display of gratitude and approval that could readily have been spared. Mr. Knightley consequently had to say how pleased he would be to see him. Mr. Weston undertook to write immediately and use every argument he could to persuade him to come.

He chose Friday, August 17th, for his manifestation and devoted most of the day to inspecting his wardrobe. At last he settled on a broad slouch hat bearing a red feather, a shroud frilled about the neck and wrists, and a rusted dagger. Toward nightfall a furious rainstorm began, with wind strong enough to shake and rattle every door and window in the ancient house. It was, in short, precisely his favourite sort of weather. This was his intended campaign. First he would slip into Washington Otis’s bedroom, gibber from the foot of the bed, and, accompanied by slow music, stab his own throat three times. He particularly resented Washington, knowing perfectly well that this was the culprit who regularly erased the celebrated Canterville bloodstain with Pinkerton’s Paragon Detergent. Once he had brought that rash and reckless youth to a state of utter terror, he would move on to the bedroom shared by the United States Minister and his wife. There he would lay a damp, cold hand upon Mrs. Otis’s brow and hiss the dreadful mysteries of the charnel-house into the ear of her quaking husband. He was less certain what to do about little Virginia. She was gentle and pretty and had never offered him any insult. He fancied a few deep groans from inside her wardrobe would be quite sufficient; should they fail to rouse her, he could scrabble at the bedspread with fingers trembling as though palsied. The twins, however, were unquestionably to receive a lesson. Naturally he must begin by sitting on their chests to give them the suffocating feeling of a nightmare. Since their beds stood near one another, he could next station himself between them as a green corpse, icy to the touch, until fright left them helpless. Finally he would discard the shroud and creep about the bedroom in bleached white bones, with a single revolving eyeball, playing ‘Dumb Daniel, or the Suicide’s Skeleton.’ He had achieved remarkable effects in that character more than once and judged it fully equal to his renowned performance as ‘Martin the Maniac, or the Masked Mystery.’

At half-past ten he heard the household retiring. For a while the twins disturbed him with shrill bursts of laughter; evidently, in the carefree spirit of schoolboys, they were entertaining themselves before settling down. By a quarter past eleven, however, everything was quiet, and when midnight struck he ventured out. An owl battered the window glass, a raven croaked in the old yew, and the wind roamed about the house with the moans of a wandering soul. Yet the Otises slept on, unaware of the fate awaiting them. Above the noise of the rain and gale, he could distinctly hear the regular snores of the Minister for the United States.
